title: Lin 211: Introduction to the Study of Language
text:
Course Description
This course is designed to give students a broad introduction to the field of linguistics from the perspective of language users. As native users of at least one spoken or signed language, students are already in some ways experts in how language works. This course will explore the beliefs about and perceptions of language that they already possess and build upon this knowledge by comparing popular notions about language with those developed in linguistic science, paying attention to the contributions of popular belief as well as the differences between them and scientific findings. [This course counts for the UK Core Inquiry in the Social Sciences requirement.]

title: Lin 211: Introduction to the Study of Language
text:
Student Learning Outcomes
After successful engagement with the material in this course, you will be able to:

Define and distinguish different theoretical approaches to linguistics,
Apply their understanding of methods and ethics of inquiry in linguistics to create and advance linguistic knowledge,
Demonstrate the ability to identify and use appropriate information resources in linguistics to substantiate evidence-based claims,
Recognize how linguistic knowledge influences society (and vice versa),
Identify well-formulated questions pertinent to linguistics and employ appropriate approaches to identify reasonable research strategies that could speak to that question.

Course Activities, Assignments, Exams

Course Activities and Exams
The following assignments will be used to determine your grade in the course. Below the descriptions, you will see the weight that each assignment type carries for your grade. Due dates for these assignments (subject to change) are listed in Canvas.

Quizzes (30%): Each week in discussion sections (beginning during the second week of classes), students will complete a short quiz in Canvas over the material that has been covered in lecture and in the course readings. These quizzes are not designed to be difficult; rather, their purpose is to ensure that everyone is keeping up with the readings and understands the material covered in the course. There will be 12 quizzes given, and the lowest two (2) quiz grades will be dropped. Each quiz is worth 3% of your final grade, for a total of 30% of the final grade. YOU WILL NEED YOUR DEVICE TO ACCESS CANVAS!
Observation notes (15%): Beginning in the second week of classes, students will keep an online language observation journal. More details will be provided, but students must listen to language as it is being used in their communities and document what they hear. It should not be necessary to record such interactions (and doing so surreptitiously would not be ok). Students will need to note the who, what, where, when, why, and how of what they heard, paying particular attention to what might make the interaction of interest to linguists. Observation is about careful and thoughtful attention to detail. Students must go beyond how they typically listen to conversations and try to listen like a linguist. There will be 6 entries to submit during the semester, and the lowest grade will be dropped. Each journal entry is worth 3% of your final grade, for a total of 15% of the final grade. YOU MUST NOT USE AI TO GENERATE THESE!
Data Collection (20%): Near the middle of the semester, students will complete a large-scale assignment involving the collection of linguistic data. More details will be provided, but students will collect data and be asked a number of questions to show that they understand aspects of linguistic research methods and ethics as explored in the class. Students will have time to work on the assignment in discussion on the due date, but the assignment will require additional time outside of class to complete. This assignment is worth 20% of the final grade.
Data Analysis (25%): Near the end of the semester, students will complete another large-scale assignment. This assignment will involve the analysis of the linguistic data collected near midterm. More details will be provided, but students will demonstrate their ability to identify an appropriate research question related to that data. Students will also provide relevant academic sources that could be used to better understand the data and the research question. Students will have time to work on the assignment during the scheduled exam time for their section, but the assignment will require additional time outside of the exam time to complete. This assignment is worth 25% of the final grade.
Participation (10%): Students are expected to attend each class (lecture and discussion) and to have done any reading or other work assigned for that day. In discussion, participation will be gauged by attendance, participation in class activities, and/or submission of assignments, as required. In lecture, participation in the class will be gauged by responses to participation questions that are sprinkled throughout the lectures. Students will be able to submit answers in class through Echo360 using a laptop, tablet, or mobile phone. The grade will be based on whether you were able to participate on a given day. If you have questions or concerns about this aspect of the course, please see the instructor immediately. Participation is worth 10% of the final grade.

Policy on the use of Generative “AI” Tools (e.g. LLMs such as ChatGPT, Claude, or Grammarly, image generators, audio/video deepfake engines, etc.)
For most assignments in this course, the use of GenAI to complete any part of the submitted work is prohibited unless explicitly specified by the instructor or TA. In the event that specific permission to use GenAI tools is given, it will (1) be explicitly stated, in writing, in the assignment, that such tools are allowed and (2) students must acknowledge any work that is not their own. The absence of either (1) explicit permission or (2) full acknowledgement by the student will be considered cheating and the student will earn zero points on the affected assignment(s). Use of these tools includes: citations for outside scholarship or information gathered from other sources, automatically paraphrasing existing work, generating text or media in response to assignment prompts, even if subsequently modified by the student, and any other use of these tools. “Full acknowledgment” means that students will, through highlighting or the use of track changes (or footnotes, etc.), clearly delineate any text or media that is generated by a GenAI tool. If you have any questions or concerns about this policy, contact your instructor before submitting any assignments. See UK-Advance instructional guidelines for more information.

title: What is linguistics?
section: Let’s start with what it does not mean
text:
Let’s start with what it does not mean

“Linguistics is the study of language”

≠ learning many languages
≠ studying a language with the goal of learning to communicate in it
≠ noticing and pointing out grammatical errors
(did you have a different meaning in mind?)

title: What is linguistics?
section: Ok, then! But what is Linguistics?!
text: Ok, then! But what is Linguistics?!

title: What is linguistics?
section: Ok, then! But what is Linguistics?!
text:
Ok, then! But what is Linguistics?!

If linguists aren’t just studying a bunch of languages or correcting people’s speech, what are they doing?
Here is a (not very useful) first definition from the Linguistic Society of America (LSA):

Linguistics is the scientific study of language. Linguists apply the scientific method to conduct formal studies of speech sounds and gestures, grammatical structures, and meaning across the world’s 6,000+ languages.
Includes the study of:

the structure of language – i.e., how do we make a sentence?
and the use of language – i.e., how do we speak with one another?

title: What is linguistics?
text:
Then what is language?!?


First – we are talking about language as an ability humans have, not any particular code.
(It’s a bit like the difference between studying the biology of frogs and dissecting a particular frog)
Second – and perhaps most importantly – the kinds of things we talk about with any individual language can be talked about for any other language because language is a feature of being human

title: What is linguistics?
text:
Example Q slide
One thing we’ll say is that all languages follow rules and that linguists try to figure out those rules. Think about times when someone has talked to you about what you can/should do with language (spoken, written, or signed). What’s a rule someone told you to follow?

title: What is linguistics?
section: We can talk about two kinds of rules
text:
We can talk about two kinds of rules

Prescriptive: probably what you’ve experienced before this class
Descriptive: what linguists do

title: What is linguistics?
text:
Pescriptive Rules

Rules are made up by external actors (e.g., teachers, grammar book writers)
The expectation is that one can write a set of rules like this and expect all language users to conform
“Don’t end a sentence with a preposition.”

title: What is linguistics?
text:
Descriptive Rules

Rules are based on observations of language in use by real language users.
Native speakers = good grammar; if a native speaker can’t say/understand it = bad grammar
“Native speakers of English put ‘the’ in front of nouns, not after.”

title: What is linguistics?
text:
Why do prescriptive rules exist?

The justification for prescriptive rules is often historically motivated, usually for absurd reasons
“Don’t split infinitives” or “Don’t end sentences in a preposition”
Why?
Because Latin doesn’t/can’t.
Wait, what?
The Latin language heavily influenced Western grammarians

title: What is linguistics?
text:
More about Prescriptive rules

Prescriptive judgments of “right” vs. “wrong” or superior vs. inferior represent learned social attitudes to a particular variety or a particular form.
They are usually judgments against the speaker groups who use those varieties rather than against the language itself.

title: What is linguistics?
text:
“Y’all”

A prescriptivist would say, “Don’t use ‘y’all’”
also: ‘ fixin ’ to’
or: [ ra:d ] vs. [raid]
These are all judgments against Southerners (not really about language) and reflect mainstream society’s view of Southern culture and people!

title: How many languages are there?
text:
What makes humans so special?





An Australian Shepherd dog




linguistics is the scientific study of language
language is the human capacity to symbolically represent thoughts, ideas, and feelings
and to experience those symbolic representations as meaning
human languages are structured systems for making articulated thoughts fully explicit
and critically depend on knowing (more or less) what the people around us know or believe, how they’re feeling, and what they might be interested in

title: How many languages are there?
text:
How are there 7,170 languages?

Most people speak at least two languages
When a group is divided, the code they share can often become so different that they become less mutually intelligible
Also, language is constantly changing. The language you speak every day would sound very strange to your great grand parents and might be genuinely difficult to understand for their great grand parents.
And sometimes we’ll arbitrarily call two mutually intelligible codes separate languages for political reasons, rather than purely linguistic ones
This kind of splitting and change creates groups of languages that are similar to each other. We call these groups of languages language families
The branches of linguistics that studies these relationship are called historical linguistics and sociolinguistics

title: What is language?
section: We can talk about two kinds of language rules
text:
We can talk about two kinds of language rules

Prescriptive: an attempt to control how language is used

⤷ very common (english teachers, grammar police, etc.)

 
Descriptive: an attempt to understand how language is used

⤷ uncommon (linguists & lexicographers)

title: What is language?
text:
Prescriptive Rules

Prescriptive Rules are made up by external actors (e.g., teachers, grammar book writers, grammar police, etc.)
That person (or group) asserts authority in language and issues a prohibition/command that is meant to be unquestioningly followed
Often they try to use shame or threats as motivation
examples:

“Don’t end a sentence with a preposition.”
“Do not use contractions.”
“It is incorrect to ever split an infinitive.
“You sound ignorant if you say ain’t.”

title: What is language?
text:
Descriptive Rules

Descriptive Rules emerge from usage and custom. Descriptive rules vest authority in the people who use and speak the language not in external authorities.

Rules are based on observations of language in use by real language users.
These rules can be broken! It is possible to say things that are ungrammatical.
It’s just that ungrammatical in the descriptive sense means “no one says that”

title: What is language?
text:
Descriptive Rules and ungrammatical examples

Example Descriptive Rule: English speakers have to use ‘the’ or ‘a/an’ before a noun.

* You must have ticket to ride train. 1
You must have a ticket to ride the train.

Example Descriptive Rule: the past tense of go is went

* Daddy goed on the airplane!
Daddy went on the airplane!


See that asterisk (*)? Linguists use it to mean ’speakers of this language can’t/don’t say this. It literally means ungrammatical.

title: What is language?
text:
Why do prescriptive rules exist?


Knowing and following descriptive rules feels right to us
It can be a way of demonstrating one’s erudition, learning, belonging, but…
Enforcing prescriptive rules can also be a way of gatekeeping who gets to be in your group
Prescriptive rules are always social judgements, not linguistic facts.

title: What is language?
text:
More about Prescriptive rules


Prescriptive judgments of “right” vs. “wrong” or superior vs. inferior represent learned social attitudes to a particular variety or a particular form.
They are usually judgments against the speaker groups who use those varieties rather than against the language itself.

How do you know what a platypus is?

How do you know what any word is?
Most people say: “look it up in the dictionary”
But that almost never happens.
Besides, dictionaries are descriptive, not prescriptive

title: What is language?
text:
Platypus



Usually, we know what a platypus (or any word!) is by combining what we already know with the evidence from the utterance to arrive at a meaning that is enough to go on
You don’t have to know that a platypus is venomous, you don’t have to know that they mammals who don’t have nipples, or that its Latin name is Ornithorhynchus anatinus to know what “I saw a platypus at the zoo” means

text:
What is language?

Last week we said we are talking about language as a distinctly human ability, not any individual language

All humans use language
Language may be spoken or signed, written or not

According to your book, “human languages are structured systems for making articulated thoughts fully explicit both internally (mentally) and externally (in a form perceptible to other humans)” (p. 3)
But that “fully explicit” depends on: who is talking, who is listening, and the context they’re in!
